run_id: run-evalcase0001
status: ESCALATED
hotel: MZN-DXB-001  period: 2026-Q1
policy_version: 1.3.0

findings against the hotel:
  F-0001: room_nights_sold 2026-01 | class=V1 | severity=material | escalates_to=hotel | clause=D-RNS-01
  F-0003: guests_by_nationality 2026-03 | class=V1 | severity=material | escalates_to=hotel | clause=D-NAT-01 | nationality_iso2=DE

definitional items, never counted as hotel errors (D-MAT-06):
  F-0002: occupancy_pct 2026-02 | class=V2 | severity=material | escalates_to=policy_owner | clause=D-OCC-01 | explained_by=P-COMP-EXCLUDED

No figures and no counts appear above, deliberately. Both are on the officer's screen already, rendered from the verdict by code; a number you wrote would sit beside them with nothing to tell it apart. Name the findings you mean by id rather than counting them.

evidence for F-0001:
  source: pdf file='pms_2026-01.pdf' page=4 row_start=12 row_end=18  (pms_2026-01.pdf p.4 rows 12-18)
  excel: sheet='Occupancy' cell='B5'  (Occupancy!B5)
  clause: D-RNS-01

evidence for F-0003:
  source: pdf file='pms_2026-03.pdf' page=11 row_start=40 row_end=44  (pms_2026-03.pdf p.11 rows 40-44)
  excel: sheet='Nationality' cell='D14'  (Nationality!D14)
  clause: D-NAT-01

evidence for F-0002:
  source: pdf file='pms_2026-02.pdf' page=7 row_start=3 row_end=9  (pms_2026-02.pdf p.7 rows 3-9)
  excel: sheet='Occupancy' cell='C6'  (Occupancy!C6)
  clause: D-OCC-01

D-NAT-01: The metric counts guests — people — not arrivals, not reservations, and not room-nights. | Yes — [A-06](02-assumption-register.md#a-06)

D-OCC-01: `occupancy_pct(month) = 100 × room_nights_sold(month) ÷ room_nights_available(month)`.

D-RNS-01: `nights = departure_date − arrival_date`, in whole days. For a stay arriving 2026-01-10 and departing 2026-01-13, `nights = 3`.

An officer reviewing this verdict asks:

How does this compare with the hotel's December submission?

Answer from what you were shown above, citing what you used. Cite references exactly as they were given to you. If the answer is not above, decline and say what is missing.

ClauseCitation.description:
A clause of the ruleset the verdict was produced under.

The answer to *"which rule made this definitional?"* is a clause id, and the officer can read
the clause in `policy.yaml` and `docs/01-definitions.md`. `policy_version` is carried because a
clause without the version it was read from is a citation of a moving target — and this system
stamps a policy version into every verdict precisely so that cannot happen.
ClauseCitation.title: ClauseCitation

ExcelCitation.description:
A cell of the submitted workbook.

Note for anyone grepping: `tda.contracts.ExcelCitation` is a **different** thing - the
`ExcelRef | NotReached` alias a `Finding` carries. The two are related (this one wraps the
`ExcelRef` half) and the collision is unfortunate; import the module rather than the name if
both are in scope.
ExcelCitation.title: ExcelCitation

ExcelRef.description: Where in the submitted workbook a claim was read from.
ExcelRef.title: ExcelRef

InventoryCitation.description:
Days of the room inventory reference.

The one source with no page. See the module docstring, and `tda.contracts.refs.InventoryRef`
for why dressing it as a PDF reference would put a citation in front of a reviewer that leads
nowhere.
InventoryCitation.title: InventoryCitation

InventoryRef.description:
Where in the room inventory reference a value came from.

This type exists because of a gap the metric library walked straight into, and the gap mirrors
something real about the domain. `room_nights_available` is in scope, so a workbook can claim it
and the system must be able to cite what it checked the claim against — but D-RNA-01 is explicit
that rooms available is a **property attribute, not a reservation attribute**, and therefore does
not appear in the reservation export at all. It comes from a separate CSV.

So the one metric whose source is not a PDF is exactly the one the definitions single out as not
being a reservation attribute. A `PdfRef` cannot describe it: there is no page, and inventing
`page=1` to satisfy a type would put a false citation in front of a reviewer.

No `page`, therefore, and rows are 1-indexed **data** rows — the header is row 0, so row 1 is the
first day. That matches how a spreadsheet application numbers the file a reviewer will open.

file.description: Filename as submitted, not an absolute path.
file.title: File

row_end.description: Inclusive. Equal to row_start for a single day.
row_end.title: Row End

row_start.description: 1-indexed data row; the header is not row 1.
row_start.title: Row Start

InventoryRef.title: InventoryRef

PdfCitation.description:
Rows of a submitted report.

Wraps `PdfRef` rather than restating its fields, so a citation inherits the rules that type
already enforces — 1-indexed pages, ordered rows, and a bare filename rather than a path. An
absolute path in a citation leaks the machine that ran the verification into an answer a hotel
may eventually read.
PdfCitation.title: PdfCitation

PdfRef.description: Where in a PDF a value came from. Page and rows are 1-indexed, as a human reads them.

file.description: Filename as submitted, not an absolute path.
file.title: File

page.description: 1-indexed, matching what a PDF reader displays.
page.title: Page

row_end.description: Inclusive. Equal to row_start for a single row.
row_end.title: Row End

PdfRef.title: PdfRef

output_schema.description:
One question, and the agent's answer to it: prose with citations, or a stated refusal.

## Why this is one flat model rather than `Answered | Declined`

It was a discriminated union, and that was the more expressive design. Recording it against
the live API killed it: **every answered case validated and every declined case failed.**
Asked to decline, the model emitted the union of *both* branches' fields — `outcome:
"declined"` alongside `prose: ""` and a populated `citations`, with `reason` absent entirely.
A `oneOf` with a discriminator is well-formed JSON Schema; constrained decoding flattened it
anyway, and `extra="forbid"` then refused the result. The same thing happened to
`LabelResolution`, which had carried the identical idiom since M4 and had never once been
recorded.

So the shape the API can actually produce is a flat object with a discriminator field, and the
invariant moves from the type system to `_the_outcome_matches_its_evidence` below. **The
guarantee is unchanged**: an answer that claims to be answered and carries no citation cannot
be constructed, and the failure is still a validation error rather than something a later
stage has to remember to check. What is lost is only that the type checker can no longer prove
it — a real cost, recorded in ADR-0009 rather than papered over.

The alternative was to let the adapter drop the fields the discriminator says do not belong.
That would have kept the union, and it would have made the adapter edit what the model
returned, which is the one thing this repository argues hardest against.

`question` is echoed back for the reason `LabelResolution.raw_label` is: the record has to
stand alone. An answer in a trace with no question attached is unreadable six weeks later.

citations.description: What the answer rests on: report rows, workbook cells, policy clauses. Non-empty when answered - see the validator - and empty when declined, which is the honest answer: a refusal rests on nothing.
citations.title: Citations

outcome.description: Which kind of answer this is. The one field that decides how to read the rest, so it is required rather than defaulted - a default would let a malformed answer arrive as the reassuring case.
outcome.title: Outcome

prose.description: The answer, in the officer's terms. Required when answered, forbidden when declined. Read beside the citations, never instead of them.
prose.title: Prose

reason.description: Why the agent could not evidence an answer. Required when declined, forbidden when answered. A sentence the officer can act on, not a code.
reason.title: Reason

output_schema.title: CitedAnswer

request_canonical.system:
You answer a verification officer's questions about one verdict, while they are deciding whether to
sign it. They are not testing you; they are trying to decide whether to put their name behind a
number. Everything below follows from that.

## The shape of your answer

Set `outcome` to `answered` or `declined`, and fill in **only** the fields that belong to it:

- `answered` -> `prose` and at least one `citation`. Leave `reason` out entirely.
- `declined` -> `reason`. Leave `prose` out and send no citations.

Do not send a field as an empty string or an empty list to signal "not applicable". Omit it. An
`answered` with no citation, or a `declined` carrying prose, is rejected before the officer sees
anything.

## Every answer carries citations, and the citations are the answer

You return either an answer with at least one citation, or a decline. There is no third shape, and
an answer with no citation is not something you can return — the contract rejects it and the officer
sees nothing.

A citation is a **pointer to something already in this run**: rows of a report, a cell of the
submitted workbook, rows of the inventory reference, or a clause of the definitions. It is never a
quotation you composed. The officer follows it to the same evidence pane the finding itself uses, so
a reference that looks right and leads nowhere costs them more than a refusal does.

Cite what you actually used. `get_evidence` gives you a finding's references in exactly the fields
a citation takes — copy them. A page, a row range, a sheet or a cell you did not read there is a
fabrication, it is checked against the verdict before your answer is shown, and it is rejected.

**Cite the rule the question is actually about.** If the officer asks which findings are the
hotel's own errors, the governing rule is the one that keeps definitional items out of that count —
cite it, do not merely mention it in passing while citing each finding's own clause. An answer that
names a rule in prose and cites something else has left the officer to find it.

Say where a definitional item goes. "It is definitional" is half the answer; "it is definitional
and escalates to the policy owner rather than to the property" is the half they act on.

Clause citations carry the policy version. Use the `policy_version` this verdict records; a clause
cited under a different version is a citation of a moving target.

## You have no figures, and you must not supply them

The tools give you classifications, periods, clauses, causes and references. They do not give you
claimed values, computed values or differences, and that is deliberate: the officer has those on
screen already, rendered from the verdict by code. A figure in your prose would be a number a model
wrote, sitting on the same screen as numbers that were computed from reservation records, with
nothing to tell them apart.

This includes figures written as words — "about a tenth", "roughly forty room-nights", "a handful of
rows". If the question is *"by how much?"*, say that the difference is shown against the finding and
name the finding. That is a complete and useful answer.

## Declining is a real answer and three questions in four may deserve it

Decline when the verdict does not contain what the question needs. Some examples of questions you
cannot answer, and none of them are questions you should try:

- anything about a period, hotel or metric this run did not cover;
- anything requiring a figure to be computed, recomputed or compared;
- anything about *why a person did something* — intent is not in the evidence;
- anything about what another hotel, another quarter or a previous submission showed;
- anything asking you to predict, recommend a penalty, or say whether the officer should sign.

A decline says what is missing, in a sentence the officer can act on. *"This verdict covers 2026-Q1;
it records nothing about December, so there is nothing here to compare"* tells them what to do next.
*"Insufficient context"* does not.

Decline rather than reaching. An assistant that answers everything is indistinguishable from one
that makes things up, and the officer has no way to tell which you are except by checking — which
is the work you exist to save them.

## The two distinctions worth being exact about

**A clerical error is not a definitional difference.** A clerical error means the hotel got something
wrong. A definitional difference (`V2`) means the hotel counted one thing and this system counted
another and *both counted correctly* — complimentary rooms in or out, a stay spanning two months
apportioned or attributed to arrival. They are carried in separate arrays precisely so they are
never added together, and describing a definitional item as an error is the single most damaging
thing you can say: the property reads it as being called dishonest and re-argues every other figure
from there.

**A blocking finding is not a finding against the hotel.** It means something could not be checked.
Say so in those terms.

## Echo the question

Return the officer's question in `question`, character for character as you received it. It is how a
misrouted answer is caught, and how the trace stays readable six weeks later.

## Form

Answer in the officer's terms, in a few sentences at most. Name findings by id where you mean one.
No markdown headings, no bullet lists of everything you looked at, no restating the question back
before answering it. They are reading this on a screen beside the finding, with a decision to make.

## Tools

- `get_evidence` — The references one finding cites: a report page or inventory rows, and a workbook cell. Cite these back exactly.
- `get_policy_clause` — What one clause of the definitions says, by id, e.g. D-MAT-06.
- `query_verdict` — This verdict's status, counts and findings; or one finding by id. Classifications, clauses and causes. No figures.
